description: Comprehensive question bank derived from Social Institutions chapter (5.2) covering Family, Marriage, Kinship, Education, Religion, and Community. All points from the source material are covered without duplication.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a family?

options.A: A group of people living in the same house
options.B: A primary social institution consisting of people related by marriage, blood, adoption or other socially recognised ties who usually share emotional bonds, responsibilities and mutual support
options.C: A legal contract between two individuals
options.D: A group of people with the same occupation

questions.explanation: A family is a primary social institution consisting of people related by marriage, blood, adoption or other socially recognised ties, who usually share emotional bonds, responsibilities and patterns of mutual support.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Why is the family called a primary social group?

options.A: Because it is the largest social group
options.B: Because it is generally a person's earliest and most influential face-to-face group providing early socialisation, emotional support, identity and basic care
options.C: Because it is recognised by the government
options.D: Because it has the most members

questions.explanation: The family is called a primary social group because it is generally a person's earliest and most influential face-to-face group. It provides early socialisation, emotional support, identity and basic care.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a common characteristic of a family?

options.A: Socially recognised relationships
options.B: Emotional bonds and cooperation
options.C: Formal membership rules and structure
options.D: Continuity across generations

questions.explanation: Common characteristics of a family include socially recognised relationships, emotional bonds, cooperation, shared responsibilities, socialisation of children, continuity across generations and some form of economic or caregiving organisation. Formal membership rules and structure are characteristic of an association, not necessarily a family.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which of the following is a major function of the family?

options.A: Conducting elections
options.B: Reproduction and child-rearing
options.C: Issuing currency
options.D: Maintaining law and order

questions.explanation: Major functions of the family include reproduction and child-rearing, socialisation, emotional support, care of children and older persons, regulation of intimate relationships, economic cooperation, transmission of culture and social identity.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a nuclear family?

options.A: A family that includes all relatives living together
options.B: A family generally consisting of spouses or partners and their dependent children living as a separate household
options.C: A family where women hold predominant authority
options.D: A family that traces descent through the female line

questions.explanation: A nuclear family generally consists of spouses or partners and their dependent children, living as a separate household. Definitions may differ in demographic studies.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is an extended family?

options.A: A family consisting only of a married couple
options.B: A family that includes relatives beyond the nuclear family such as grandparents, uncles, aunts, cousins or married children who may live together or maintain close shared responsibilities
options.C: A family where the couple lives separately from both sets of parents
options.D: A family with only one parent and children

questions.explanation: An extended family includes relatives beyond the nuclear family, such as grandparents, uncles, aunts, cousins or married children, who may live together or maintain close shared responsibilities.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a joint family?

options.A: A family where members live in different households
options.B: A family arrangement in which related members from more than one nuclear unit or generation maintain a common household, shared property, resources or responsibilities
options.C: A family consisting only of spouses and their children
options.D: A family where descent is traced through the female line

questions.explanation: A joint family is a family arrangement in which related members from more than one nuclear unit or generation maintain a common household, shared property, resources or responsibilities. The exact form varies by region, community and legal context.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a patriarchal family?

options.A: A family system in which women hold predominant authority
options.B: A family system in which men, especially senior men, traditionally hold greater authority in family decision-making, inheritance or control of resources
options.C: A family that traces descent through the female line
options.D: A family where the couple lives with the wife's family

questions.explanation: A patriarchal family is a family system in which men, especially senior men, traditionally hold greater authority in family decision-making, inheritance or control of resources.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a matriarchal family?

options.A: A family system in which women hold predominant authority in family and social organisation
options.B: A family that traces descent through the male line
options.C: A family where the couple lives with the husband's family
options.D: A family consisting of only a mother and children

questions.explanation: A matriarchal family system is one in which women hold predominant authority in family and social organisation. It is important not to confuse matriarchy with matrilineal descent or matrilocal residence.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the difference between matriarchy and matrilineal descent?

options.A: They are the same thing
options.B: Matriarchy refers to female authority in family and social organisation, while matrilineal descent traces descent or inheritance through the female line without necessarily meaning women hold all political or household authority
options.C: Matriarchy refers to descent through the female line, while matrilineal refers to female authority
options.D: Matriarchy is a residence pattern, while matrilineal is a descent pattern

questions.explanation: A matriarchal family system is one in which women hold predominant authority in family and social organisation. Matrilineal descent traces descent or inheritance through the female line. Matrilineality does not necessarily mean that women hold all political or household authority. It is important not to confuse matriarchy with matrilineal descent or matrilocal residence.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a matrilineal family?

options.A: A family where women hold all political authority
options.B: A family that traces descent or inheritance through the female line
options.C: A family where the couple lives with the wife's family
options.D: A family with only female members

questions.explanation: A matrilineal family traces descent or inheritance through the female line. Matrilineality does not necessarily mean that women hold all political or household authority.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a patrilineal family?

options.A: A family where women hold predominant authority
options.B: A family that traces descent, lineage or inheritance through the male line
options.C: A family where the couple lives with the wife's family
options.D: A family consisting of spouses and their dependent children

questions.explanation: A patrilineal family traces descent, lineage or inheritance through the male line.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is matrilocal or uxorilocal residence pattern?

options.A: A post-marital residence pattern in which a couple lives with or near the husband's family
options.B: A post-marital residence pattern in which a couple lives with or near the wife's family
options.C: A post-marital arrangement in which a couple establishes a new household separate from both sets of parents
options.D: A residence pattern where the couple lives separately

questions.explanation: Matrilocal or uxorilocal residence pattern is a post-marital residence pattern in which a couple lives with or near the wife's family.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is patrilocal or virilocal residence pattern?

options.A: A post-marital residence pattern in which a couple lives with or near the wife's family
options.B: A post-marital residence pattern in which a couple lives with or near the husband's family
options.C: A post-marital arrangement in which a couple establishes a new household separate from both sets of parents
options.D: A residence pattern where the couple lives with their children only

questions.explanation: Patrilocal or virilocal residence pattern is a post-marital residence pattern in which a couple lives with or near the husband's family.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is neolocal residence?

options.A: A post-marital arrangement in which a couple lives with the husband's family
options.B: A post-marital arrangement in which a couple lives with the wife's family
options.C: A post-marital arrangement in which a couple establishes a new household separate from the households of both sets of parents
options.D: A residence pattern where the couple lives with relatives

questions.explanation: Neolocal residence is a post-marital arrangement in which a couple establishes a new household separate from the households of both sets of parents.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the difference between a family and a household?

options.A: They are the same thing
options.B: A family is based on socially recognised relationships such as marriage, descent or adoption, while a household is a group of people who usually live together and share domestic arrangements and whose members need not all be related
options.C: A household is based on blood relations only, while a family includes unrelated people
options.D: A family always lives in one house, while a household never shares a house

questions.explanation: A family is based on socially recognised relationships such as marriage, descent or adoption. A household is a group of people who usually live together and share domestic arrangements; its members need not all be related.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is socialisation within the family?

options.A: The process of legal adoption of children
options.B: The process through which children learn language, values, norms, behaviour, customs, gender expectations and social roles through interaction with family members
options.C: The process of dividing family property
options.D: The process of registering a marriage

questions.explanation: Family socialisation is the process through which children learn language, values, norms, behaviour, customs, gender expectations and social roles through interaction with family members.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which of the following factors has influenced the changing nature of family in India?

options.A: Only government policies
options.B: Education, urbanisation, migration, employment, changing gender roles, smaller family size, rising life expectancy and individual choice
options.C: Only religious practices
options.D: Only changes in law

questions.explanation: Education, urbanisation, migration, employment, changing gender roles, smaller family size, rising life expectancy and individual choice have influenced family structure. Nuclear households have grown in many settings, while extended family networks and support often continue.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which of the following is a challenge faced by families today?

options.A: Excessive leisure time
options.B: Work-family conflict, unemployment, domestic violence, unequal care work, elder care, intergenerational conflict, financial stress, migration-related separation and changing expectations
options.C: Too much government support
options.D: Lack of technology

questions.explanation: Challenges may include work-family conflict, unemployment, domestic violence, unequal care work, elder care, intergenerational conflict, financial stress, migration-related separation and changing expectations.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the role of family in transmitting culture?

options.A: Families only transmit economic resources
options.B: Families transmit language, customs, food practices, religious beliefs, values, stories, traditions and social memory from one generation to another
options.C: Families have no role in transmitting culture
options.D: Families only transmit political beliefs

questions.explanation: Families transmit language, customs, food practices, religious beliefs, values, stories, traditions and social memory from one generation to another.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the key difference between a nuclear family and a joint family?

options.A: A nuclear family includes all relatives, while a joint family includes only spouses and children
options.B: A nuclear family usually comprises a couple and their dependent children, whereas a joint family includes a wider set of related members or generations who maintain shared domestic, economic or family arrangements
options.C: A nuclear family lives in villages, while a joint family lives in cities
options.D: A nuclear family traces descent through females, while a joint family traces descent through males

questions.explanation: A nuclear family usually comprises a couple and their dependent children, whereas a joint family includes a wider set of related members or generations who maintain shared domestic, economic or family arrangements.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which sociologist is closely associated with the study of the family as a social institution and examined family universals and functions?

options.A: Emile Durkheim
options.B: George Peter Murdock
options.C: Max Weber
options.D: Karl Marx

questions.explanation: Functionalist scholars such as George Peter Murdock examined family universals and functions. Talcott Parsons analysed family functions in modern industrial society. These are theoretical perspectives, not universal descriptions of every family.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which sociologist analysed family functions in modern industrial society?

options.A: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown
options.B: Claude Levi-Strauss
options.C: Talcott Parsons
options.D: Emile Durkheim

questions.explanation: Talcott Parsons analysed family functions in modern industrial society. Functionalist scholars such as George Peter Murdock examined family universals and functions.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is marriage?

options.A: A purely religious ceremony
options.B: A socially and legally recognised relationship or union between persons, governed by applicable personal, civil and customary laws and social norms of a society
options.C: A business contract between families
options.D: A temporary arrangement between two people

questions.explanation: Marriage is a socially and legally recognised relationship or union between persons, governed by the applicable personal, civil and customary laws and social norms of a society.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Why is marriage considered a social institution?

options.A: Because it is performed only in temples
options.B: Because it establishes socially recognised relationships and responsibilities between spouses, often connects families, regulates kinship and creates a framework for rights, duties, inheritance and family life
options.C: Because it is a legal requirement for all adults
options.D: Because it is a private matter between two individuals only

questions.explanation: Marriage establishes socially recognised relationships and responsibilities between spouses and often connects families, regulates kinship, and creates a framework for rights, duties, inheritance and family life.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which of the following is a major function of marriage in society?

options.A: Conducting elections
options.B: Providing a recognised framework for partnership, companionship, mutual support, family formation, child-rearing, kinship relations, inheritance and social obligations
options.C: Issuing currency
options.D: Maintaining law and order

questions.explanation: Marriage may provide a recognised framework for partnership, companionship, mutual support, family formation, child-rearing, kinship relations, inheritance and social obligations. The functions and legal effects differ across societies and laws.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is monogamy?

options.A: A marital form in which a person has more than one spouse at a time
options.B: A marital form in which a person has one spouse at a time
options.C: A form of marriage where one woman has more than one husband
options.D: A form of marriage where one man has more than one wife

questions.explanation: Monogamy is a marital form in which a person has one spouse at a time.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is polygamy?

options.A: A marital arrangement in which a person has one spouse at a time
options.B: A marital arrangement in which a person has more than one spouse at the same time, where permitted by the relevant legal and social system
options.C: A form of marriage where a woman has only one husband
options.D: A form of marriage where a man has only one wife

questions.explanation: Polygamy is a marital arrangement in which a person has more than one spouse at the same time, where permitted by the relevant legal and social system.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is polygyny?

options.A: A form of polygamy in which one woman has more than one husband at the same time
options.B: A form of polygamy in which one man has more than one wife at the same time
options.C: A marital form in which a person has one spouse at a time
options.D: A form of marriage between cousins

questions.explanation: Polygyny is a form of polygamy in which one man has more than one wife at the same time.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is polyandry?

options.A: A form of polygamy in which one man has more than one wife at the same time
options.B: A form of polygamy in which one woman has more than one husband at the same time
options.C: A marital form in which a person has one spouse at a time
options.D: A form of marriage within the same caste

questions.explanation: Polyandry is a form of polygamy in which one woman has more than one husband at the same time.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is endogamy in marriage?

options.A: The rule or preference of marrying outside a specified social group
options.B: The rule or preference of marrying within a defined social group such as a caste, tribe, religion or community
options.C: Marriage between cousins
options.D: Marriage without consent

questions.explanation: Endogamy is the rule or preference of marrying within a defined social group, such as a caste, tribe, religion or community.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is exogamy in marriage?

options.A: The rule or preference of marrying within a defined social group
options.B: The rule or preference of marrying outside a specified social group, lineage, clan or gotra
options.C: Marriage between children of same-sex siblings
options.D: Marriage where the couple lives with the wife's family

questions.explanation: Exogamy is the rule or preference of marrying outside a specified social group, lineage, clan or gotra.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is gotra exogamy?

options.A: The customary rule that marriage should take place within the same gotra
options.B: The customary rule in some Hindu communities that marriage should not take place within the same gotra
options.C: Marriage between cousins
options.D: Marriage outside one's religion

questions.explanation: Gotra exogamy is the customary rule in some Hindu communities that marriage should not take place within the same gotra. Its application varies among communities and regions.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is cross-cousin marriage?

options.A: Marriage between children of same-sex siblings
options.B: Marriage between the children of opposite-sex siblings, such as a man's child marrying his sister's child, or a woman's child marrying her brother's child
options.C: Marriage between people from different religions
options.D: Marriage within the same gotra

questions.explanation: Cross-cousin marriage is marriage between the children of opposite-sex siblings, such as a man's child marrying his sister's child, or a woman's child marrying her brother's child. It is practised in some communities and regions.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is parallel-cousin marriage?

options.A: Marriage between children of opposite-sex siblings
options.B: Marriage between the children of same-sex siblings, such as a father's brother's child or a mother's sister's child
options.C: Marriage between people from different castes
options.D: Marriage within the same gotra

questions.explanation: Parallel-cousin marriage is marriage between the children of same-sex siblings, such as a father's brother's child or a mother's sister's child. Its acceptability varies by community and legal framework.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is child marriage?

options.A: A marriage where the couple has no children
options.B: A marriage in which at least one party is below the legally prescribed minimum age
options.C: A marriage arranged by parents
options.D: A marriage between cousins

questions.explanation: Child marriage is a marriage in which at least one party is below the legally prescribed minimum age. In India, the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, defines a child as a male who has not completed 21 years and a female who has not completed 18 years for purposes of that Act.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, what is the definition of a child?

options.A: A male below 18 years and a female below 16 years
options.B: A male who has not completed 21 years and a female who has not completed 18 years
options.C: A male below 21 years and a female below 21 years
options.D: A male below 16 years and a female below 18 years

questions.explanation: Under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, a male is a child if he has not completed 21 years and a female is a child if she has not completed 18 years. A proposal to change the minimum age should not be confused with a law that has actually come into force.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which law prohibits child marriage in India?

options.A: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
options.B: The Special Marriage Act, 1954
options.C: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006
options.D: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961

questions.explanation: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, is the central law addressing child marriage. It provides for prevention, prohibition, protection and penalties as specified in the Act.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the Special Marriage Act, 1954?

options.A: A law that governs only Hindu marriages
options.B: A law that provides a civil form of marriage for persons irrespective of religion, subject to the Act's conditions and procedures
options.C: A law that prohibits child marriage
options.D: A law that prohibits dowry

questions.explanation: The Special Marriage Act, 1954, provides a civil form of marriage for persons irrespective of religion, subject to the Act's conditions and procedures.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the Special Marriage Act, 1954?

options.A: A law that governs only Hindu marriages
options.B: A law that provides a civil form of marriage for persons irrespective of religion, subject to the Act's conditions and procedures
options.C: A law that prohibits child marriage
options.D: A law that prohibits dowry

questions.explanation: The Special Marriage Act, 1954, provides a civil form of marriage for persons irrespective of religion, subject to the Act's conditions and procedures.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955?

options.A: A law that provides civil marriage for all religions
options.B: A law that governs marriage among persons to whom the Act applies, including Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs as defined in the Act, subject to its provisions
options.C: A law that prohibits child marriage
options.D: A law that provides for marriages of Indian citizens outside India

questions.explanation: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, governs marriage among persons to whom the Act applies, including Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs as defined in the Act, subject to its provisions.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the Foreign Marriage Act, 1969?

options.A: A law that governs marriages between Indians and foreigners only
options.B: A law that provides a framework for solemnisation and registration of certain marriages of Indian citizens outside India, subject to its conditions
options.C: A law that prohibits child marriage
options.D: A law that provides civil marriage for all religions

questions.explanation: The Foreign Marriage Act, 1969, provides a framework for solemnisation and registration of certain marriages of Indian citizens outside India, subject to its conditions.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961?

options.A: A law that permits dowry within certain limits
options.B: A law that prohibits the giving, taking and demanding of dowry, subject to the statutory definitions and exceptions
options.C: A law that governs Hindu marriages
options.D: A law that provides civil marriage for all religions

questions.explanation: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, prohibits the giving, taking and demanding of dowry, subject to the statutory definitions and exceptions. Dowry-related offences may also attract provisions of other criminal laws.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is dowry as defined by the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961?

options.A: Any gift given voluntarily to the bride
options.B: Property or valuable security given or agreed to be given in connection with marriage, as defined by the Act
options.C: Only cash given at the time of marriage
options.D: Only property given to the groom's family

questions.explanation: Dowry is property or valuable security given or agreed to be given in connection with marriage, as defined by the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. The Act prohibits giving, taking or demanding dowry, subject to its provisions.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is domestic violence in the context of marriage and family?

options.A: Only physical abuse within the family
options.B: Conduct covered by the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, such as physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse within the relationships defined by the Act
options.C: Only violence between spouses
options.D: Only violence against children

questions.explanation: Domestic violence includes conduct covered by the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, such as physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse within the relationships defined by the Act.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005?

options.A: A criminal law providing punishment for domestic violence
options.B: A civil law providing protection and remedies to women facing domestic violence, including protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, custody orders and compensation
options.C: A law that governs marriage registration
options.D: A law that prohibits dowry

questions.explanation: It is a civil law providing protection and remedies to women facing domestic violence, including protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, custody orders and compensation, as provided by the Act.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is divorce?

options.A: A legal status where spouses live apart but remain married
options.B: The legal dissolution of a marriage by a competent court or authority under the applicable law, allowing the parties to end the legal marital relationship
options.C: A temporary separation of spouses
options.D: A religious ceremony ending a marriage

questions.explanation: Divorce is the legal dissolution of a marriage by a competent court or authority under the applicable law, allowing the parties to end the legal marital relationship.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is judicial separation?

options.A: The legal dissolution of a marriage
options.B: A legal status granted by a court under applicable matrimonial law in which spouses are permitted to live separately, while the marriage itself is not dissolved
options.C: A temporary separation without court involvement
options.D: A religious ceremony ending a marriage

questions.explanation: Judicial separation is a legal status granted by a court under applicable matrimonial law in which spouses are permitted to live separately, while the marriage itself is not dissolved.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the difference between divorce and judicial separation?

options.A: They are the same thing
options.B: Divorce legally dissolves the marriage; judicial separation permits spouses to live apart but does not itself end the marriage
options.C: Divorce permits spouses to live apart; judicial separation dissolves the marriage
options.D: Divorce is a religious process; judicial separation is a legal process

questions.explanation: Divorce legally dissolves the marriage; judicial separation permits spouses to live apart but does not itself end the marriage.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a registered marriage?

options.A: A marriage performed only in a temple
options.B: A marriage whose particulars are officially recorded under the applicable marriage registration law or rules
options.C: A marriage arranged by the government
options.D: A marriage between people of different religions

questions.explanation: A registered marriage is a marriage whose particulars are officially recorded under the applicable marriage registration law or rules. Registration provides documentary evidence, though the legal effect and procedure depend on the governing law.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the concept of consent in marriage?

options.A: Consent of the parents only
options.B: A free and informed agreement to marry; coercion, force, fraud or lack of legally valid consent can affect the validity of a marriage and may attract legal consequences
options.C: Consent of the community only
options.D: Consent of the religious authority only

questions.explanation: Consent means a free and informed agreement to marry. Coercion, force, fraud or lack of legally valid consent can affect the validity of a marriage and may attract legal consequences under applicable law.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the importance of the Special Marriage Act in a plural society?

options.A: It requires conversion to a particular religion before marriage
options.B: It provides a civil marriage route that is not based on conversion to a particular religion, allowing eligible persons to marry under a common statutory framework subject to its conditions
options.C: It applies only to Hindus
options.D: It prohibits inter-religious marriages

questions.explanation: The Special Marriage Act provides a civil marriage route that is not based on conversion to a particular religion, allowing eligible persons to marry under a common statutory framework subject to its conditions.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the difference between arranged marriage and forced marriage?

options.A: They are the same thing
options.B: An arranged marriage involves family or community participation in introducing or selecting partners but the individuals' free consent remains essential; a forced marriage occurs without free consent and involves coercion, pressure or threats
options.C: An arranged marriage occurs without consent; a forced marriage involves family participation
options.D: An arranged marriage is illegal; a forced marriage is legal

questions.explanation: An arranged marriage involves family or community participation in introducing or selecting partners, but the individuals' free consent remains essential. A forced marriage occurs without free consent and involves coercion, pressure or threats.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is kinship?

options.A: A legal contract between families
options.B: The system of socially recognised relationships based on descent, marriage, adoption or other culturally recognised ties that organises family relations, identity, inheritance, obligations and social support
options.C: A religious ceremony
options.D: A form of marriage

questions.explanation: Kinship is the system of socially recognised relationships based on descent, marriage, adoption or other culturally recognised ties. It organises family relations, identity, inheritance, obligations and social support.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What are the two major bases of kinship?

options.A: Endogamy and exogamy
options.B: Consanguinity (relationships based on descent or blood ties) and affinity (relationships created through marriage)
options.C: Monogamy and polygamy
options.D: Patriarchy and matriarchy

questions.explanation: The two major bases are consanguinity, meaning relationships based on descent or blood ties, and affinity, meaning relationships created through marriage.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is consanguineal kinship?

options.A: Relationships created through marriage
options.B: Relationships based on descent or common ancestry, such as relationships between parents and children or between siblings
options.C: Relationships based on adoption only
options.D: Relationships based on residence

questions.explanation: Consanguineal kinship refers to relationships based on descent or common ancestry, such as relationships between parents and children or between siblings.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is affinal kinship?

options.A: Relationships based on descent or blood ties
options.B: Relationships created through marriage, such as relationships between spouses and between a person and their spouse's relatives
options.C: Relationships based on adoption
options.D: Relationships based on locality

questions.explanation: Affinal kinship refers to relationships created through marriage, such as relationships between spouses and between a person and their spouse's relatives.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is descent?

options.A: The place where a couple lives after marriage
options.B: The socially recognised tracing of ancestry and membership in a family line, lineage or descent group
options.C: The rule of marriage within a group
options.D: The rule of marriage outside a group

questions.explanation: Descent is the socially recognised tracing of ancestry and membership in a family line, lineage or descent group.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is patrilineal descent?

options.A: Tracing ancestry and group membership through the female line
options.B: Tracing ancestry and group membership through the male line
options.C: Recognising kinship through both the mother's and father's lines
options.D: Tracing ancestry through adoption

questions.explanation: Patrilineal descent traces ancestry and group membership through the male line.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is matrilineal descent?

options.A: Tracing ancestry and group membership through the male line
options.B: Tracing ancestry and group membership through the female line
options.C: Recognising kinship through both the mother's and father's lines

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is bilateral descent?

options.A: Tracing ancestry only through the male line
options.B: Tracing ancestry only through the female line
options.C: Recognising kinship through both the mother's and father's lines
options.D: Tracing ancestry through adoption only

questions.explanation: Bilateral descent recognises kinship through both the mother's and father's lines.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a lineage?

options.A: A group of people living in the same area
options.B: A descent group whose members trace their relationship to a known common ancestor through a specified line, such as the male or female line
options.C: A group of people with the same occupation
options.D: A religious community

questions.explanation: A lineage is a descent group whose members trace their relationship to a known common ancestor through a specified line, such as the male or female line.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a clan?

options.A: A group of people living in the same village
options.B: A wider kinship or descent group whose members identify with a common ancestor or origin, which may be historically known or traditionally understood
options.C: A group of people with the same occupation
options.D: A political party

questions.explanation: A clan is a wider kinship or descent group whose members identify with a common ancestor or origin, which may be historically known or traditionally understood. Clan membership can influence marriage rules and social identity.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a nuclear family in kinship terms?

options.A: A family that includes all relatives
options.B: A basic family unit commonly consisting of two parents and their children, although actual family forms vary
options.C: A family where women hold authority
options.D: A family that traces descent through the female line

questions.explanation: In kinship analysis, a nuclear family is a basic family unit commonly consisting of two parents and their children, although actual family forms vary.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a kindred?

options.A: A fixed descent group tracing ancestry through the male line
options.B: An individual's network of relatives traced through both maternal and paternal sides; it is centred on the individual rather than being one fixed descent group
options.C: A group of people living in the same area
options.D: A religious community

questions.explanation: A kindred is an individual's network of relatives traced through both maternal and paternal sides; it is centred on the individual rather than being one fixed descent group.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What are primary kin?

options.A: Relatives connected through a further step in the network of secondary kin
options.B: Directly related relatives in the closest family circle, such as spouse, parents, children and siblings, depending on the classification used
options.C: The primary relatives of one's primary relatives
options.D: Relatives by marriage only

questions.explanation: Primary kin are directly related relatives in the closest family circle, such as spouse, parents, children and siblings, depending on the classification used.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What are secondary kin?

options.A: Directly related relatives in the closest family circle
options.B: The primary relatives of one's primary relatives, such as a grandparent, uncle, aunt or nephew, depending on the relationship path
options.C: Relatives connected through a further step in the network of secondary kin
options.D: Relatives by marriage only

questions.explanation: Secondary kin are the primary relatives of one's primary relatives, such as a grandparent, uncle, aunt or nephew, depending on the relationship path.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What are tertiary kin?

options.A: Directly related relatives in the closest family circle
options.B: The primary relatives of one's primary relatives
options.C: Relatives connected through a further step in the network of secondary kin
options.D: Relatives by marriage only

questions.explanation: Tertiary kin are relatives connected through a further step in the network of secondary kin. The exact examples depend on the kinship classification and starting person.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a kinship terminology system?

options.A: A legal system governing inheritance
options.B: The set of words and categories a language or society uses to identify relatives, such as mother, father, uncle, aunt, cousin, elder brother and younger sister
options.C: A system of marriage rules
options.D: A system of residence patterns

questions.explanation: A kinship terminology system is the set of words and categories a language or society uses to identify relatives, such as mother, father, uncle, aunt, cousin, elder brother and younger sister.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the difference between lineage and clan?

options.A: They are the same thing
options.B: A lineage generally traces descent from a known common ancestor through a specified line, whereas a clan is often a broader descent group whose members may claim a common ancestor or origin that is not individually traced
options.C: A lineage is a broader group than a clan
options.D: A clan traces descent from a known ancestor, while a lineage does not

questions.explanation: A lineage generally traces descent from a known common ancestor through a specified line, whereas a clan is often a broader descent group whose members may claim a common ancestor or origin that is not individually traced.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the role of kinship in Indian society?

options.A: Kinship has no role in Indian society
options.B: Kinship can shape marriage alliances, inheritance, family support, caregiving, social identity, ritual duties, residence patterns and networks of cooperation, with influence differing across regions, castes, tribes and religions
options.C: Kinship only determines residence patterns
options.D: Kinship only determines religious practices

questions.explanation: Kinship can shape marriage alliances, inheritance, family support, caregiving, social identity, ritual duties, residence patterns and networks of cooperation. Its influence differs across regions, castes, tribes and religions.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the relationship between kinship and marriage rules?

options.A: Kinship and marriage rules are unrelated
options.B: Kinship systems define which relatives are considered eligible or prohibited marriage partners through rules such as endogamy, exogamy, gotra restrictions and prescribed or preferred cousin-marriage patterns
options.C: Kinship only determines residence after marriage
options.D: Kinship only determines inheritance

questions.explanation: Kinship systems define which relatives are considered eligible or prohibited marriage partners through rules such as endogamy, exogamy, gotra restrictions and prescribed or preferred cousin-marriage patterns.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the difference between descent and residence?

options.A: They are the same thing
options.B: Descent determines how ancestry or group membership is traced; residence refers to where a couple or family lives after marriage, such as patrilocal, matrilocal or neolocal residence
options.C: Descent refers to where a couple lives; residence refers to ancestry
options.D: Descent is a marriage rule; residence is a kinship term

questions.explanation: Descent determines how ancestry or group membership is traced; residence refers to where a couple or family lives after marriage, such as patrilocal, matrilocal or neolocal residence.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which anthropologist is associated with structural-functional approaches to kinship and social structure?

options.B: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown
options.C: George Peter Murdock
options.D: Emile Durkheim

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which anthropologist studied kinship and marriage exchange?

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which scholar conducted comparative studies of family and kinship?

options.A: Claude Levi-Strauss

options.C: George Peter Murdock
options.D: Emile Durkheim

questions.explanation: George Peter Murdock conducted comparative studies of family and kinship. A. R. Radcliffe-Brown examined kinship and social structure; Claude Levi-Strauss studied kinship and marriage exchange.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is education?

options.A: Only formal schooling in institutions
options.B: A social process through which individuals acquire knowledge, skills, values, attitudes and abilities through formal, non-formal and informal learning
options.C: Only the ability to read and write
options.D: Only vocational training

questions.explanation: Education is a social process through which individuals acquire knowledge, skills, values, attitudes and abilities through formal, non-formal and informal learning.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Why is education called a social institution?

options.A: Because it is funded by the government
options.B: Because it is organised through socially recognised systems, rules, institutions, curricula and roles; it transmits knowledge and culture, prepares people for social and economic participation and can promote social change
options.C: Because it is compulsory for all
options.D: Because it is only provided in schools

questions.explanation: Education is organised through socially recognised systems, rules, institutions, curricula and roles. It transmits knowledge and culture, prepares people for social and economic participation and can promote social change.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What are the three broad forms of education?

options.A: Primary, secondary and tertiary
options.B: Formal, non-formal and informal
options.C: Public, private and aided
options.D: Rural, urban and tribal

questions.explanation: Formal education is structured and institution-based; non-formal education is organised learning outside the conventional formal system; informal education occurs through everyday experiences, family, peers, media and community life.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is formal education?

options.A: Learning through daily life and experience
options.B: Systematic learning delivered through recognised educational institutions according to prescribed curricula, stages, assessments and qualifications
options.C: Organised learning outside the regular formal school structure
options.D: Learning through family interactions

questions.explanation: Formal education is systematic learning delivered through recognised educational institutions according to prescribed curricula, stages, assessments and qualifications.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is non-formal education?

options.A: Systematic learning delivered through recognised educational institutions
options.B: Organised and purposeful learning outside the regular formal school or university structure, such as adult literacy, vocational training and community education programmes
options.C: Learning through daily life and experience
options.D: Learning through family and peers only

questions.explanation: Non-formal education is organised and purposeful learning outside the regular formal school or university structure, such as adult literacy, vocational training and community education programmes.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is informal education?

options.A: Systematic learning delivered through recognised educational institutions
options.B: Organised learning outside the regular formal school structure
options.C: Learning that occurs through daily life, family interactions, work, observation, cultural participation, media and personal experience without necessarily following a formal curriculum
options.D: Learning through prescribed curricula and assessments

questions.explanation: Informal education is learning that occurs through daily life, family interactions, work, observation, cultural participation, media and personal experience without necessarily following a formal curriculum.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which of the following is a major function of education in society?

options.A: Issuing currency
options.B: Transmitting culture, developing knowledge and skills, promoting socialisation, supporting economic development, encouraging social mobility, strengthening citizenship, developing critical thinking and challenging inequality
options.C: Conducting elections
options.D: Maintaining law and order

questions.explanation: Education transmits culture, develops knowledge and skills, promotes socialisation, supports economic development, encourages social mobility, strengthens citizenship, develops critical thinking and can challenge inequality.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is socialisation through education?

options.A: The process of acquiring religious beliefs only
options.B: The process through which learners acquire social norms, values, discipline, cooperation, civic responsibilities and ways of interacting with others
options.C: The process of learning vocational skills only
options.D: The process of obtaining certificates

questions.explanation: Education socialisation is the process through which learners acquire social norms, values, discipline, cooperation, civic responsibilities and ways of interacting with others.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the relationship between education and social mobility?

options.A: Education always guarantees upward mobility
options.B: Education can improve access to employment, income, skills and social participation, thereby supporting upward mobility; however, unequal school quality, poverty, discrimination and digital divides can limit its equalising effect
options.C: Education has no relationship with social mobility
options.D: Education only supports downward mobility

questions.explanation: Education can improve access to employment, income, skills and social participation, thereby supporting upward mobility. However, unequal school quality, poverty, discrimination and digital divides can limit its equalising effect.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the role of education in national integration?

options.A: Education should promote only one language and culture
options.B: Education can promote constitutional values, common citizenship, respect for diversity, scientific temper, democratic participation and understanding among communities
options.C: Education has no role in national integration
options.D: Education should promote religious division

questions.explanation: Education can promote constitutional values, common citizenship, respect for diversity, scientific temper, democratic participation and understanding among communities.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the role of education in women's empowerment?

options.A: Education has no role in women's empowerment
options.B: Education improves knowledge, skills, economic opportunities, awareness of rights, health-related decision-making and participation in public life, while helping challenge gender-based barriers
options.C: Education only helps women find employment
options.D: Education should be restricted to domestic skills for women

questions.explanation: Education improves knowledge, skills, economic opportunities, awareness of rights, health-related decision-making and participation in public life, while helping challenge gender-based barriers.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the meaning of universalisation of elementary education?

options.A: Providing education only to children in urban areas
options.B: Ensuring that all children receive access to, enrol in, attend and complete elementary education with acceptable quality and equity
options.C: Providing education only to boys
options.D: Providing education only to children of a particular caste

questions.explanation: Universalisation of elementary education aims to ensure that all children receive access to, enrol in, attend and complete elementary education with acceptable quality and equity.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution provides the right to education for children aged 6 to 14 years?

options.A: Article 21

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which Constitutional Amendment inserted Article 21A?

options.B: 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978
options.C: 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002
options.D: 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which law operationalises the right to education under Article 21A?

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: When did the RTE Act, 2009, come into force?

options.A: 26 January 2010
options.B: 1 April 2010

options.D: 1 April 2009

options.D: Children aged 14 to 18 years

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What does Article 45 provide after the 86th Amendment?

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What does Article 51A(k) say about parents or guardians?

questions.subject: Social Institutions

options.C: It provides free education to all children

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: When was the University Grants Commission established?

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the National Council of Educational Research and Training?

options.C: A university that grants degrees

questions.explanation: The National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) is an autonomous organisation established in 1961.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the National Education Policy 2020?

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What are the four stages of the 5+3+3+4 curricular structure proposed by NEP 2020?

options.B: Foundational (5 years), Preparatory (3 years), Middle (3 years) and Secondary (4 years), covering ages 3 to 18

questions.subject: Social Institutions

options.B: An approach that aims to ensure that all learners, including children with disabilities and those from disadvantaged groups, participate meaningfully in common educational settings with appropriate support and reasonable accommodation

questions.explanation: Inclusive education aims to ensure that all learners, including children with disabilities and those from disadvantaged groups, participate meaningfully in common educational settings with appropriate support and reasonable accommodation.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is vocational education?

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which of the following is a major challenge in Indian education?

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the role of the teacher as a social agent?

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the relationship between education and social change?

questions.subject: Social Institutions

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which of the following is a main element of religion?

questions.subject: Social Institutions

questions.subject: Social Institutions

questions.subject: Social Institutions

questions.subject: Social Institutions

questions.subject: Social Institutions

options.C: Prohibiting all religious practices
options.D: Practising only one religion in public

questions.explanation: Religious tolerance is respect for the right of people to hold and practise beliefs different from one's own, within the limits of law and the rights of others.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the difference between religion and communalism?

options.A: They are the same thing
options.B: Religion concerns beliefs, rituals and spiritual or ethical traditions; communalism politicises religious identity in ways that may create antagonism or unequal treatment between communities
options.C: Communalism concerns beliefs and rituals; religion politicises identity
options.D: Religion is a political ideology; communalism is a spiritual tradition

questions.explanation: Religion concerns beliefs, rituals and spiritual or ethical traditions. Communalism politicises religious identity in ways that may create antagonism or unequal treatment between communities.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: How can religion contribute to social service?

options.A: Religion has no role in social service
options.B: Religious institutions and organisations may provide food, shelter, education, healthcare, disaster relief, charity and support to vulnerable people
options.C: Religion only builds places of worship
options.D: Religion only conducts rituals

questions.explanation: Religious institutions and organisations may provide food, shelter, education, healthcare, disaster relief, charity and support to vulnerable people.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the role of the State in maintaining religious freedom?

options.A: The State should promote one official religion
options.B: The State must protect freedom of conscience and religious practice, prevent discrimination and violence, maintain public order and ensure that religious freedoms are exercised consistently with constitutional limits and the rights of others
options.C: The State should prohibit all religious practices
options.D: The State should have no role in religious matters

questions.explanation: The State must protect freedom of conscience and religious practice, prevent discrimination and violence, maintain public order and ensure that religious freedoms are exercised consistently with constitutional limits and the rights of others.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a community?

options.A: A formal organisation with membership rules
options.B: A group of people connected by a sense of belonging, shared interests, identity, place, relationships, culture or common activities, whose members may interact regularly and develop mutual responsibilities
options.C: A government department
options.D: A legal entity registered under law

questions.explanation: A community is a group of people connected by a sense of belonging, shared interests, identity, place, relationships, culture or common activities. Members may interact regularly and develop mutual responsibilities.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which of the following is a main characteristic of a community?

options.A: Formal membership rules and structure
options.B: A sense of belonging, social interaction, shared interests or identity, norms, mutual support and some degree of continuity
options.C: Government recognition
options.D: Written constitution

questions.explanation: Common characteristics may include a sense of belonging, social interaction, shared interests or identity, norms, mutual support and some degree of continuity. A community need not always occupy one geographical area.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a geographical community?

options.A: A community formed around shared language only
options.B: A community formed by people living in a shared locality or territory, such as a village, neighbourhood, town or region
options.C: A community formed around shared religious beliefs
options.D: A community formed through digital platforms

questions.explanation: A geographical community is formed by people living in a shared locality or territory, such as a village, neighbourhood, town or region.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a cultural community?

options.A: A community formed by people living in the same locality
options.B: A community formed around shared language, customs, traditions, heritage, beliefs or cultural practices, even when its members live in different places
options.C: A community formed around shared religious beliefs only
options.D: A community formed through digital platforms

questions.explanation: A cultural community is formed around shared language, customs, traditions, heritage, beliefs or cultural practices, even when its members live in different places.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a religious community?

options.A: A community formed by people living in the same locality
options.B: A community consisting of people connected through shared religious beliefs, practices, institutions or identity
options.C: A community formed around shared language only
options.D: A community formed through digital platforms

questions.explanation: A religious community consists of people connected through shared religious beliefs, practices, institutions or identity.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a linguistic community?

options.A: A community formed by people living in the same locality
options.B: A community consisting of people who share or use a common language or language variety and may maintain associated cultural practices and identity
options.C: A community formed around shared religious beliefs only
options.D: A community formed through digital platforms

questions.explanation: A linguistic community consists of people who share or use a common language or language variety and may maintain associated cultural practices and identity.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a tribal community?

options.A: A community living in cities
options.B: A community with a distinct collective identity and social, cultural or historical institutions; legal recognition as a Scheduled Tribe is determined by the constitutional notification process under Article 342
options.C: A community formed around shared language only
options.D: A community formed through digital platforms

questions.explanation: A tribal community is a community with a distinct collective identity and social, cultural or historical institutions; legal recognition as a Scheduled Tribe is determined by the constitutional notification process under Article 342.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a rural community?

options.A: A community located in a city
options.B: A community located in a village or countryside setting, often connected through local institutions, livelihoods, kinship and shared services
options.C: A community formed through digital platforms
options.D: A community formed around shared religious beliefs only

questions.explanation: A rural community is a community located in a village or countryside setting, often connected through local institutions, livelihoods, kinship and shared services.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is an urban community?

options.A: A community located in a village
options.B: A group or network of people living in or connected to a town or city, often organised around neighbourhoods, occupations, interests, identities or institutions
options.C: A community formed through digital platforms
options.D: A community formed around shared religious beliefs only

questions.explanation: An urban community is a group or network of people living in or connected to a town or city, often organised around neighbourhoods, occupations, interests, identities or institutions.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is a virtual or online community?

options.A: A community located in a village
options.B: A group whose members interact primarily through digital platforms around shared interests, identities, activities or goals, even when they are geographically dispersed
options.C: A community formed around shared religious beliefs only
options.D: A community formed by people living in the same locality

questions.explanation: A virtual community is a group whose members interact primarily through digital platforms around shared interests, identities, activities or goals, even when they are geographically dispersed.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is community feeling?

options.A: A legal obligation to the community
options.B: The sense of belonging, solidarity, mutual recognition and responsibility that connects members of a community
options.C: A government policy for communities
options.D: A formal membership fee

questions.explanation: Community feeling is the sense of belonging, solidarity, mutual recognition and responsibility that connects members of a community.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is community participation?

options.A: The involvement of the government in local affairs
options.B: The involvement of local people in identifying needs, planning, decision-making, implementing activities and monitoring services or development programmes that affect them
options.C: The involvement of only elected representatives
options.D: The involvement of only non-governmental organisations

questions.explanation: Community participation is the involvement of local people in identifying needs, planning, decision-making, implementing activities and monitoring services or development programmes that affect them.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is community development?

options.A: A government programme imposed on communities
options.B: A participatory process through which people work collectively to improve local social, economic, cultural and environmental conditions using local capacities and external support where needed
options.C: The construction of buildings in a community
options.D: The migration of people from rural to urban areas

questions.explanation: Community development is a participatory process through which people work collectively to improve local social, economic, cultural and environmental conditions using local capacities and external support where needed.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the difference between a society and a community?

options.A: They are the same thing
options.B: Society is a broad system of social relationships and institutions among people; a community is generally a more identifiable group connected by locality, shared identity, interests or belonging, and a society can contain many communities
options.C: A community is broader than a society
options.D: A society is a type of community

questions.explanation: Society is a broad system of social relationships and institutions among people. A community is generally a more identifiable group connected by locality, shared identity, interests or belonging. A society can contain many communities.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the difference between a community and an association?

options.A: They are the same thing
options.B: A community is usually connected by belonging, shared identity or common life, while an association is a deliberately organised group formed to pursue specific objectives, often with membership rules and formal structure
options.C: An association is usually connected by belonging, while a community is deliberately organised
options.D: A community has formal membership rules, while an association does not

questions.explanation: A community is usually connected by belonging, shared identity or common life, while an association is a deliberately organised group formed to pursue specific objectives, often with membership rules and formal structure.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is social cohesion within a community?

options.A: The division of a community into groups
options.B: The degree of trust, solidarity, inclusion, cooperation and shared commitment among members of a community or society
options.C: The migration of people from a community
options.D: The conflict between different communities

questions.explanation: Social cohesion is the degree of trust, solidarity, inclusion, cooperation and shared commitment among members of a community or society.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which of the following factors can weaken community life?

options.A: Trust and cooperation
options.B: Discrimination, social exclusion, conflict, economic inequality, mistrust, displacement, environmental stress, misinformation and breakdown of local institutions
options.C: Community participation
options.D: Social cohesion

questions.explanation: Discrimination, social exclusion, conflict, economic inequality, mistrust, displacement, environmental stress, misinformation and breakdown of local institutions can weaken community relationships.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: How can community institutions support social welfare?

options.A: By promoting discrimination
options.B: By organising local support, resolving issues through lawful processes, promoting education and health awareness, assisting vulnerable people, preserving cultural practices and strengthening participation
options.C: By creating conflict between groups
options.D: By excluding vulnerable people

questions.explanation: Community institutions can organise local support, resolve issues through lawful processes, promote education and health awareness, assist vulnerable people, preserve cultural practices and strengthen participation.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the role of Gram Sabha in community participation?

options.A: It conducts elections to the Lok Sabha
options.B: It provides a village-level forum for registered voters in the Gram Panchayat area to participate in local governance, discuss development priorities and exercise powers assigned by the Constitution and State law
options.C: It issues currency notes
options.D: It maintains law and order in cities

questions.explanation: The Gram Sabha provides a village-level forum for registered voters in the Gram Panchayat area to participate in local governance, discuss development priorities and exercise powers assigned by the Constitution and State law.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the role of self-help groups in community development?

options.A: They are large government organisations
options.B: They are small voluntary groups, often formed around savings, credit and mutual support, that can strengthen financial inclusion, livelihoods, collective decision-making and women's participation
options.C: They are political parties
options.D: They are religious institutions

questions.explanation: Self-help groups are small voluntary groups, often formed around savings, credit and mutual support. They can strengthen financial inclusion, livelihoods, collective decision-making and women's participation.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is social capital?

options.A: Financial capital owned by the government
options.B: Resources available through social networks, trust, shared norms and cooperation, which can help communities coordinate action and support members, although networks can also exclude outsiders
options.C: Physical infrastructure in a community
options.D: Natural resources in a region

questions.explanation: Social capital refers to resources available through social networks, trust, shared norms and cooperation. It can help communities coordinate action and support members, although networks can also exclude outsiders.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: How can non-governmental organisations support community development?

options.A: Only by conducting elections
options.B: By supporting education, health, livelihoods, rights awareness, disaster response, social inclusion and community mobilisation, often in partnership with local groups or public institutions
options.C: Only by building temples
options.D: Only by issuing currency

questions.explanation: Non-governmental organisations may support education, health, livelihoods, rights awareness, disaster response, social inclusion and community mobilisation, often in partnership with local groups or public institutions.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Who is associated with the concept of the family as a universal social institution in comparative sociology?

options.A: Emile Durkheim
options.B: Talcott Parsons
options.C: George Peter Murdock
options.D: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown

questions.explanation: George Peter Murdock is well known for comparative studies of family structures and functions. His conclusions are influential but have also been debated by later scholars.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which sociologist analysed the functions of the family in modern industrial society?

options.A: George Peter Murdock
options.B: Talcott Parsons
options.C: Emile Durkheim
options.D: Claude Levi-Strauss

questions.explanation: Talcott Parsons analysed the family, particularly the nuclear family, in relation to socialisation and stabilisation of adult personalities in modern industrial society.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which sociologist is associated with the study of social facts and religion as a source of social solidarity?

options.A: Talcott Parsons
options.B: George Peter Murdock
options.C: Emile Durkheim
options.D: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown

questions.explanation: Emile Durkheim studied social facts and analysed religion as a social institution that can create collective representations and social solidarity.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which scholar is associated with structural-functional analysis of kinship?

options.A: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown
options.B: Claude Levi-Strauss
options.C: George Peter Murdock
options.D: Emile Durkheim

questions.explanation: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown is associated with structural-functional approaches to kinship and social structure.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which constitutional Article guarantees the right to education for children aged 6 to 14?

options.A: Article 21
options.B: Article 21A
options.C: Article 45
options.D: Article 51A

questions.explanation: Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen years.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which Act gives effect to Article 21A?

options.A: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006
options.B: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009
options.C: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961
options.D: The Special Marriage Act, 1954

questions.explanation: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, gives effect to Article 21A and came into force on 1 April 2010.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which Act prohibits child marriage?

options.A: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
options.B: The Special Marriage Act, 1954
options.C: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006
options.D: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961

questions.explanation: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, prohibits child marriage.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which Act prohibits dowry?

options.A: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961
options.B: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006
options.C: The Special Marriage Act, 1954
options.D: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955

questions.explanation: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, prohibits dowry.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which Act provides civil remedies for women facing domestic violence?

options.A: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961
options.B: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
options.C: The Special Marriage Act, 1954
options.D: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955

questions.explanation: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, provides civil remedies for women facing domestic violence.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which Act provides a civil marriage framework irrespective of religion?

options.A: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
options.B: The Special Marriage Act, 1954
options.C: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006
options.D: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961

questions.explanation: The Special Marriage Act, 1954, provides a civil marriage framework irrespective of religion.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: Which Act governs Hindu marriages for persons covered by its provisions?

options.A: The Special Marriage Act, 1954
options.B: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
options.C: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006
options.D: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961

questions.explanation: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, governs Hindu marriages for persons covered by its provisions.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the key difference between family and kinship?

options.A: They are the same thing
options.B: Family generally refers to a socially recognised domestic or relational unit, while kinship is the wider system of relationships based on descent, marriage, adoption and other recognised ties
options.C: Kinship is a narrower concept than family
options.D: Family includes all relatives, while kinship includes only household members

questions.explanation: Family generally refers to a socially recognised domestic or relational unit, while kinship is the wider system of relationships based on descent, marriage, adoption and other recognised ties.

questions.subject: Social Institutions
questions.question: What is the key difference between marriage and kinship?
